summary: A 1976 paper that outlines a high-level framework for sharing resources across a network, rather than only specifying low-level protocols. It suggests programmers call remote services in a uniform way, building on resource sharing as the goal of the ARPANET.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 707 proposes a shared way for application programs to invoke functions on other computers. A common protocol and local runtime environment would reduce the repeated work needed to use remote resources.

questions: what is the framework proposed in rfc 707
how would a remote procedure call work in rfc 707
what does the proposed runtime environment do
subtitle: A framework for making remote resources easier for programs to use and combine.

tldr.problem: Each function-oriented network protocol repeats command and response machinery, leaving application programmers to build similar runtime support for every remote service.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 707 proposes isolating a common command/response protocol and providing a local runtime environment, then models remote commands as procedure calls with arguments, outcomes and results.
tldr.outcome: The paper outlines a protocol and programming model intended to encourage programs to use remote resources and build distributed systems.

today: The unit records RFC 707's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. The paper proposes a high-level network protocol and run-time environment for distributed resource sharing.

sections.title: From Human Sessions to Program Access
sections.content:
The RFC identifies resource sharing as the goal of connecting computers. Existing approaches use protocols such as TELNET for people and function-oriented protocols such as FTP and RJE for programs. In TELNET, the human-facing command language remains specific to each remote system, making it difficult for programs to use those services as building blocks.

The author argues that program-to-program resource access can make remote resources easier to combine and use. The paper assumes an interprocess communication facility and focuses on higher-level protocol design.
sections.plainLanguage: Remote users can type commands into another system, but programs cannot easily use those same human-oriented commands. The paper proposes a more structured way for programs to access remote services.

sections.title: Separating the Common Command/Response Rules
sections.content:
FTP, RJE and related protocols share a command/response pattern: a process sends a named command with parameters, and a server returns a numbered response and explanatory text. RFC 707 says this common discipline has been repeated separately in each application protocol.

The paper proposes isolating that discipline in an application-independent protocol. A single installation-maintained run-time environment could then format commands, use interprocess communication, parse responses and provide an interface that applications can reuse.
sections.plainLanguage: Several network protocols use the same basic exchange: send a command and get a reply. The paper proposes one shared mechanism so every application does not have to build it again.

sections.title: Commands, Results and Transactions
sections.content:
The proposed protocol defines COMMAND messages containing a command name and arguments, and RESPONSE messages containing an outcome and results. An optional transaction identifier (TID) links a command to its response. A failed command can return an error number and diagnostic text.

The design calls for multiple parameters and data types, results as well as arguments, commands in either direction, concurrent outstanding commands and the ability to suppress an unnecessary response. Parameters would use primitive types such as lists, character strings, bit strings, integers, indexes, booleans and empty placeholders.
sections.plainLanguage: A command can carry several typed arguments, and its response can return results. A transaction identifier lets a program match each reply to the command that caused it.

sections.title: Remote Procedures and a Run-Time Environment
sections.content:
The paper's proposed model treats a remote resource as a collection of procedures. A program can call a named procedure on another machine, pass arguments and receive an outcome and results. The author suggests that compilers might support remote calls and that a local run-time environment would handle the network messages.

The paper cautions that remote calls cost much more than local calls and do not require suspending the caller: the run-time environment could provide blocking and non-blocking modes. It also says that not every useful network interaction fits procedure calls, so the underlying interprocess communication facility remains available.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal makes remote functions look more like local procedures, while recognizing that a network call costs more. Programs can continue running while a remote call is in progress, or wait for it to finish.
